summary: Specifies RADIUS attributes for authorizing management access to a Network Access Server, both local and remote, with granular access rights and management privileges. There are special provisions for remote management.

eli5.summary: Before letting someone fix a network machine, a gatekeeper decides what they may touch. This gives the gatekeeper a language for that.

questions: what is framed management in radius
subtitle: New RADIUS attributes that say who may manage a network device, over which protocol, how securely, and with what privileges.

tldr.problem: RADIUS could only say 'console-style command line access, privileged or not'. Devices now offer more privilege levels and other management tools such as web interfaces, SNMP and NETCONF, and RADIUS had no way to authorize them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a Framed-Management value for Service-Type and four attributes: Framed-Management-Protocol (133), Management-Transport-Protection (134), Management-Policy-Id (135) and Management-Privilege-Level (136).
tldr.outcome: A RADIUS server can now tell a device which management protocol to allow, how strongly the transport must be protected, and which named policy or privilege level applies. This is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Framed-Management-Protocol values
facts.value: 8 assigned (SNMP, Web-based, NETCONF, FTP, TFTP, SFTP, RCP, SCP)

today: RFC 5607 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. RFC 5608 builds on it to describe RADIUS use with SNMP transport models.

sections.title: Why Management Access Needed New Attributes
sections.content:
RFC 2865 defined the NAS-Prompt (7) and Administrative (6) values of the Service-Type (6) attribute. Both give access to the text-based command line interface (CLI) of a Network Access Server (NAS), and were first meant for the physical console port, usually a serial port.

Remote CLI access later arrived through Telnet, Rlogin and SSH. To tell local from remote, a NAS typically sends NAS-Port-Type (61) with Async (0) for a serial port or Virtual (5) for a remote session. That gives no way to choose among the remote protocols.

The RFC notes that devices now commonly have more than two privilege levels, and that other management mechanisms exist: web-based management, SNMP and NETCONF. It therefore defines attributes for Framed Management protocols, management protocol security and privilege levels. Framed Management means protocols that carry management data in a format such as HTML, XML or ASN.1/BER, as opposed to a terminal session.
sections.eli5: The old system only had two keys: a small one and a big one. Now there are many doors and many kinds of keys, so the gatekeeper needs a richer way to say who gets what.

sections.title: Overview of the New Pieces
sections.content:
The RFC adds one new value to an existing attribute and four new attributes:

  • Service-Type value Framed-Management (18): start a Framed Management protocol session on the NAS.
  • Framed-Management-Protocol (133): which management protocol to use.
  • Management-Transport-Protection (134): the minimum transport protection required.
  • Management-Policy-Id (135): the name of a pre-provisioned management policy.
  • Management-Privilege-Level (136): an integer privilege level for CLI management.

The policy-name attribute works like Filter-Id (11) from RFC 2865: the RADIUS server names something the NAS already has configured. The local policy might be a command privilege level, a mapping into an SNMP access control model such as the View-based Access Control Model (VACM), or some other rule set both sides understand.

The RFC also treats integrity protection and authentication as separate concerns. It assumes authentication always happens before an Access-Accept is sent, so the SNMP idea of noAuth has no analog here.
sections.eli5: It is like a form with a few new boxes: which door, how locked the hallway must be, which rulebook applies and how high a level of trust to give.

sections.title: Framed-Management-Protocol and Transport Protection
sections.content:
Framed-Management-Protocol (133) names the management protocol for the session. The NAS is RECOMMENDED to send it, along with Service-Type = Framed-Management, in an Access-Request as a hint; the server MAY use them in its decision. The server MAY put the attribute in an Access-Accept to enforce one form of access. If the NAS cannot deliver that protocol, or the user asked for a different one, the NAS MUST treat the Access-Accept as an Access-Reject.

The value is a four-octet enumeration, with other values reserved for IANA: SNMP (1), Web-based (2), NETCONF (3), FTP (4), TFTP (5), SFTP (6), RCP (7) and SCP (8). The last five are file-transfer tools used to move configuration files.

Management-Transport-Protection (134) sets the minimum protection for the remote management transport. The NAS MAY provide more but MUST NOT provide less. Its values are No-Protection (1), Integrity-Protection (2) and Integrity-Confidentiality-Protection (3). The last one requires both protection from unauthorized modification (a cryptographic checksum) and from disclosure (encryption). Omitting the attribute means the same as No-Protection. The attribute does not apply to a local serial port, and the RFC leaves the choice of cipher suites and keys out of scope.

If the NAS cannot meet the required protection, it MUST treat the Access-Accept as an Access-Reject.
sections.eli5: The gatekeeper can say 'use the web page, and only through the locked tunnel'. If the guest cannot do exactly that, the door stays shut.

sections.title: Policy Names and Privilege Levels
sections.content:
Management-Policy-Id (135) carries the name of a management access policy. Zero or one instance MAY appear in an Access-Accept. The NAS MUST apply the named policy to the authorized session; if the name is unknown or the policy rules are badly formatted, it MUST treat the Access-Accept as an Access-Reject. The policy itself is configured on the NAS by other means (the RFC mentions SNMP, NETCONF or CLI), and the name is local to that NAS.

The name is a flat string, not parsed by the receiver. The RFC says splitting it into multi-part specifiers such as Access=remote, Level=7 SHOULD NOT be done, and recommends a Vendor Specific (26) attribute instead if a plain name is not enough. Several instances have no defined precedence, so they SHOULD NOT be sent.

Management-Privilege-Level (136) is a four-octet integer. What each value means is vendor specific, though the RFC recommends that greater numbers imply greater privilege. It is RECOMMENDED for sessions with Service-Type NAS-Prompt (7), where it raises the minimum privilege, and NOT RECOMMENDED with Administrative (6). It is also NOT RECOMMENDED to combine it with Management-Policy-Id or to use it for anything but interactive CLI.
sections.eli5: A policy name is like a badge that says 'Library Helper', and the building already knows what that badge allows. A privilege level is a number on the badge, where bigger usually means more access.

sections.title: Attribute Groupings and Dynamic Authorization
sections.content:
Section 8 gives nine example groupings. For instance, fully protected CLI access at privilege level 15 uses Service-Type = NAS-Prompt (7), NAS-Port-Type = Virtual (5), Management-Transport-Protection = Integrity-Confidentiality-Protection (3) and Management-Privilege-Level = 15. Secure web access with a custom level uses Framed-Management (18), Web-based (2), protection value 3 and a Management-Policy-Id of "Read-only web access". For the SNMP policy example, the RFC says there is no standardized way yet to map such a policy within SNMP.

Use with Dynamic Authorization (RFC 5176) is entirely OPTIONAL. To find an existing management session, the primary identifiers SHOULD be User-Name (1) and Service-Type (6), with extra NAS-held identifiers such as Acct-Session-Id (44) where those are not enough. In a Change-of-Authorization request, only the policy and privilege level attributes may appear, and they replace the existing values.
sections.eli5: The examples are like sample hall passes: 'main door, locked hallway, level 15' or 'web page only, read only'.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Proxies
sections.content:
The new attributes are protected by the same RADIUS and Diameter mechanisms as other attributes, which guard against spoofing and tampering in transit. They do not stop an authorized server or proxy from inserting attributes with bad intent.

A legacy NAS that does not know these attributes may silently discard them while still granting CLI access for NAS-Prompt or Administrative. A user could then get access, or a higher level, than intended. Servers SHOULD try to find out whether the NAS supports the attributes before sending them.

If a NAS cannot tell what protection its transport provides, it MUST treat an Access-Accept with a protection value other than No-Protection (1) as an Access-Reject, unless local policy overrides this. Using No-Protection is NOT RECOMMENDED where secure management is required.

In proxy chains, the RFC points out that the NAS owner should control who can provision management access. Options include using only local, non-proxy servers for management requests, or having the first-hop proxy filter such attributes coming from upstream proxies not run by the NAS owner. Passwords are also visible in cleartext at each proxy, since RADIUS protects them only hop by hop.
sections.eli5: An old guard who has never seen the new badges might wave everybody through. So the gatekeeper should check the guard knows the new rules, and should not pass messages through strangers.

sections.title: IANA Assignments and Diameter
sections.content:
IANA assigned Framed-Management (18) as a new Service-Type value and attribute types 133 to 136. Additional enumerated values for the new attributes follow RFC 3575, with the added requirement of a published specification.

In Diameter, the attributes are used as AVPs from the 1-255 RADIUS attribute compatibility space, so no new Diameter codes are allocated. Gateways between RADIUS and Diameter copy them as is, apart from changes in headers, alignment and padding.
sections.eli5: The numbers on the new badges were officially registered so everyone uses the same ones.

items.label: Web-based
items.desc: Embedded web server in the NAS, HTML over HTTP or HTTPS.

items.label: NETCONF
items.desc: XML over supported transports such as SSH, BEEP or SOAP.

items.label: FTP
items.desc: Transfers configuration files to and from the NAS.

items.label: TFTP
items.desc: Transfers configuration files to and from the NAS.

items.label: SFTP
items.desc: Securely transfers configuration files, using SSH.

items.label: RCP
items.desc: Remote copy utility for configuration files.

items.label: SCP
items.desc: Secure copy utility, a wrapper around SSH.

items.label: No-Protection
items.desc: No transport protection required; any supported transport is accepted.

items.label: Integrity-Protection
items.desc: Transport must protect against modification using a cryptographic checksum.

items.label: Integrity-Confidentiality-Protection
items.desc: Transport must provide integrity protection and encryption.

items.title: Framed-Management-Protocol (133)
items.text: Which management protocol the session may use.

items.title: Management-Policy-Id (135)
items.text: Name of a policy already configured on the NAS.

items.title: Management-Privilege-Level (136)
items.text: Integer privilege level for CLI access.
